title: SETI Scans Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS for Alien Tech—and Finds a Blueprint for Future Searches
summary: What if a chunk of another solar system carried more than just rock and ice? That tantalizing question drove SETI researchers to train the Allen Telescope Array on 3I/ATLAS, only the third confirmed interstellar object to pass through our neighborhood. Discovered in July 2025, this comet-like body offered a rare opportunity: if it were artificial—a derelict probe or active beacon—it might emit narrowband radio signals, the kind nature never produces. Over seven hours, the team scanned frequencies from 1 to 9 gigahertz, sifting through nearly 74 million candidate signals. The vast majority were instantly recognizable as human-made interference. After filtering out Earth-based sources and matching signals to the object's motion, just 200 candidates remained—and every one was traced back to our own technology. 'The results from 3I/ATLAS show how realistic it is to detect a signal with the technology we have today,' said co-author Valeria Garcia Lopez. The null result reinforces the natural origin of 3I/ATLAS, but the exercise was far from fruitless. It established that any transmitter on or near the object must be weaker than about 10–110 watts—comparable to a household appliance—across the observed bands. More importantly, the observations began less than 24 hours after the object's discovery was announced, showcasing the Allen Telescope Array's rapid-response capability. 'Eventually, our own Voyager spacecraft will be extraterrestrial artifacts in other stellar systems,' noted lead author Dr. Sofia Sheikh. 'It is important that we understand the natural distribution of interstellar objects so that we will be able to identify any anomalies.' As new telescopes come online, astronomers expect to find more such visitors. Each one offers a double prize: a chance to study material from another star and a target to practice the search for technosignatures. This study, while finding no aliens, provides a template for how to quickly and thoroughly vet the next interstellar wanderer—and perhaps one day, to answer the age-old question of whether we are alone.
why_it_matters: Even without finding aliens, this study establishes a rapid-response playbook for vetting the next interstellar visitor. As more powerful telescopes spot more such objects, today's students could be the ones analyzing data that forces us to reconsider our place in the universe.

background_read: The first known interstellar visitor, 'Oumuamua, was spotted in 2017, and a second, the comet Borisov, in 2019. Both sparked debates about whether they might be alien artifacts rather than natural rocks.

The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) has traditionally listened for deliberate signals from distant stars, but interstellar objects offer a new target: they could be probes sent across the galaxy, similar to the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft (launched in 1977, now traveling through interstellar space).

The Allen Telescope Array, a dedicated radio observatory in California funded partly by the SETI Institute, is designed for rapid-response observations, able to pivot and lock onto newly discovered objects within hours.

3I/ATLAS was discovered in July 2025 and immediately flagged for SETI scans. This study tested the ability to react quickly, filter out interference from Earth, and set strict limits on any artificial transmitter—a practice run for the day a more suspicious visitor appears.

perspectives.description: Proponents argue that every interstellar object is a free sample from another star system; even a null SETI result teaches us about the object's composition and the limits of alien technology. The test proved we can react quickly enough to catch a fleeting signal.

Critics point out that scanning for radio whispers from a specific object is a long shot given the vastness of space and unknown alien technology. The effort might divert attention from more systematic surveys of the entire sky for general technosignatures.

Historically, the search for extraterrestrial intelligence has shifted from listening to entire star systems to targeted approaches; this study fits into a decades-long evolution of strategy. It also parallels the study of meteorites: just as we learned to recognize rocks from Mars, we are learning to recognize potentially artificial visitors from other stars.

If future telescopes like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory find dozens of interstellar objects per year, rapid-response protocols will be essential. A next step could involve deploying space-based sensors to intercept and analyze an object up close, or to set tighter limits on artificial transmitters.
